opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the most underrated parts of the problem. People tend to imagine a device in a single context: alone at their desk, or walking around talking to it. Real life isn't like that. You move constantly between being alone, being with your family, sitting in a meeting, riding a crowded train. A device that's meant to be a companion has to behave well across all of those.

In private you might want something very conversational, where you think out loud and it has rich context about you. In public that can be awkward or inappropriate. You may not want to speak aloud, and you definitely don't want it surfacing something personal in front of other people. So it needs a sense of social context, almost the way a thoughtful person adjusts how they talk depending on who's in the room.

There's also the question of the people around you who never opted in. If something is aware of its surroundings, you have to think hard about privacy for bystanders, not just the user. Getting that wrong would undermine trust in the whole category, and I think trust is the main thing.

So when we think about new form factors, the question isn't only whether something is magical when you're alone with it. It's whether it's polite, discreet, and still useful when you're out in the world. If you can nail both, you get something people want with them all the time. If you only nail one, it ends up in a drawer.

r001.rationale: The response explains that private use may be conversational and context-rich, while public use may call for discretion and avoiding spoken or personal disclosures.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's one of the most underrated constraints, honestly. When we think about what a new device should be, the easy mistake is to design for one context. You design for the person sitting at their desk, or you design for the person walking down the street, and you end up with something that feels great in one place and slightly wrong everywhere else.

But people don't live in one context. You wake up at home, you're on the train, you're in a meeting, you're at dinner with friends, you're alone again at night. The same person, the same intent, wildly different social norms about what's acceptable. Talking out loud to a device in your kitchen is totally fine. Talking out loud to it in a quiet restaurant is not. Having something glance at your screen in private is fine. Having it visible on a crowded subway is a different thing.

So the question we keep asking ourselves is: what does it mean for a device to be genuinely ambient? Something that can be with you all day without ever making you feel self-conscious or making the people around you uncomfortable. I think that's actually a very hard design problem, and it's as much about social intelligence as it is about hardware. The device has to understand, or at least be gracefully usable in, the fact that you're not always in a place where you can speak, or look at a screen, or be seen interacting with it.

And there's a trust dimension too. In public, the people around you didn't opt in. So the device has to be respectful of that. It should be obvious to others when it's paying attention and when it's not. I think if we get that right, people will accept these things into their lives in a way that feels natural. If we get it wrong, it doesn't matter how capable the model is, nobody will want to carry it. The phone succeeded partly because it works everywhere. I think the next thing has to clear that bar, and probably a higher one, because it'll be far more capable and far more personal.

r001.rationale: It explains that acceptable device interactions vary by setting, contrasting speaking aloud at home with doing so in a quiet restaurant and describing different norms in public and private.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s really important. You want something that fits into your life, and your life happens in both public and private. At home, talking out loud to an AI might feel totally natural. In a crowded elevator, it probably won’t—and you may not want the answer spoken out loud either.

So the device has to give you different ways to interact and make it clear what it’s hearing, what it’s sharing, and what other people can see. If you’re constantly having to think about whether it’s appropriate to use, that’s a lot of friction. The challenge is making it useful across those settings while keeping you in control.

r001.rationale: The response says a device should offer different ways to interact across public and private settings, with speaking aloud natural at home but unsuitable in a crowded elevator.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s pretty important. A device like this has to fit into your life, and your life moves between private and public spaces all day. At home, you might be comfortable talking to it out loud and giving it more context. In a meeting or on a crowded train, you need a different way to interact with it, and different expectations about what it can hear or see.

The challenge is making that transition feel natural while keeping you in control. And it has to make sense to the people around you, too. If using it makes everyone else uncomfortable, that’s a real limitation, even if the device is useful to you.

r001.rationale: The response says a person may interact with the device aloud at home but need a different way to interact in a meeting or crowded train, identifying different uses across private and public settings.
